data.name: Rapamycin
data.description: Sirolimus; mTORC1 inhibitor that acts as a complex with FKBP12. With chronic dosing it can also disrupt mTORC2 assembly in some cell types and tissues (SAR2006; mouse liver in LAM2012), a time- and cell-type-dependent effect. Immunosuppressant; extends lifespan in mice.
data.description_beginner: Also called sirolimus. The original mTOR-blocking drug (mainly hits mTORC1; with long-term use it can also affect mTORC2 in some tissues). Used to prevent organ-transplant rejection, and the most reproducibly lifespan-extending drug in mice across the testing sites of the NIA programme.

reading_levels.beginner: The drug that made this pathway famous.
reading_levels.student: Allosteric mTORC1 inhibitor that works only as a complex with FKBP12.
reading_levels.research: Sirolimus. Not an active-site inhibitor: the FKBP12–rapamycin complex binds the FRB domain and partially occludes substrate access, which is why 4E-BP1 phosphorylation is only incompletely blocked.

studies.title: RAFT1: a mammalian protein that binds to FKBP12 in a rapamycin-dependent fashion and is homologous to yeast TORs
studies.authors: Sabatini DM; Erdjument-Bromage H; Lui M; Tempst P; Snyder SH

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Discovery of the protein RAFT1 (today's mTOR) as the direct target of the FKBP12-rapamycin complex; one of three 1994 reports (with Brown et al. and Chiu et al.) that identified mammalian TOR, three years after TOR was found in yeast.

studies.title: Rapamycin fed late in life extends lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice
studies.authors: Harrison DE; Strong R; Sharp ZD; Nelson JF; Astle CM; Flurkey K; Nadon NL; Wilkinson JE; Frenkel K; Carter CS; Pahor M; Javors MA; Fernandez E; Miller RA

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Rapamycin fed from 600 days of age extended median and maximal lifespan in both sexes; age at 90% mortality rose 14% in females and 9% in males.

studies.title: Rapamycin-induced insulin resistance is mediated by mTORC2 loss and uncoupled from longevity
studies.authors: Lamming DW; Ye L; Katajisto P; Goncalves MD; Saitoh M; Stevens DM; Davis JG; Salmon AB; Richardson A; Ahima RS; Guertin DA; Sabatini DM; Baur JA

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Mouse (in vivo glucose and insulin tolerance)
studies.finding: Chronic rapamycin (about 2 mg/kg a day, close to the lifespan-extending dose) made mice glucose intolerant and insulin resistant. A clamp test placed the problem in the liver, which kept making glucose, while muscle and fat took up glucose normally. Removing mTORC1 from the liver did not cause this. Rapamycin did break up mTORC2 (it separated mTOR from Rictor) in liver, fat and muscle, and deleting Rictor in the liver alone reproduced the glucose problem. In the genetic part, female mice with one working copy each of mTOR and mLST8 had about 50% less mTORC1 signalling in the liver, normal mTORC2 signalling and normal glucose tolerance, and lived 14.4% longer on average (p = 0.046). Males did not. Boundary: mouse drug and genetics work, not people, and the lifespan gain is female-only. It supports separating the two effects, but the paper does not test a drug that blocks mTORC1 without touching mTORC2.

studies.title: Rapamycin, but not resveratrol or simvastatin, extends life span of genetically heterogeneous mice
studies.authors: Miller RA; Harrison DE; Astle CM; Baur JA; Boyd AR; de Cabo R; Fernandez E; Flurkey K; Javors MA; Nelson JF; Orihuela CJ; Pletcher S; Sharp ZD; Sinclair D; Starnes JW; Wilkinson JE; Nadon NL; Strong R
studies.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: In the same experimental design that showed rapamycin extended median lifespan by 10-18%, neither resveratrol nor simvastatin had any significant effect on survival - a direct head-to-head negative control run at the same time, in the same mice.

studies.title: Rapamycin (AY-22,989), a new antifungal antibiotic. I. Taxonomy of the producing streptomycete and isolation of the active principle
studies.authors: Vézina C; Kudelski A; Sehgal SN

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: The original isolation of rapamycin from a soil bacterium found on Easter Island, discovered first as an antifungal compound decades before its mTOR-inhibiting mechanism was known.

studies.title: Targets for cell cycle arrest by the immunosuppressant rapamycin in yeast
studies.authors: Heitman J; Movva NR; Hall MN

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Discovery of the TOR1 and TOR2 genes in yeast as the targets whose disruption causes rapamycin's cell-cycle-arresting toxicity - the original genetic identification of the TOR pathway.

studies.title: Mechanisms of life span extension by rapamycin in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster
studies.authors: Bjedov I; Toivonen JM; Kerr F; Slack C; Jacobson J; Foley A; Partridge L

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Feeding rapamycin extended fly lifespan through autophagy and reduced translation, and worked even in flies already on a lifespan-maximizing diet.

studies.title: Transient rapamycin treatment can increase lifespan and healthspan in middle-aged mice
studies.authors: Bitto A; Ito TK; Pineda VV; LeTexier NJ; Huang HZ; Sutlief E; Tung H; Vizzini N; Chen B; Smith K; Meza D; Yajima M; Beyer RP; Kerr KF; Davis DJ; Gillespie CH; Snyder JM; Treuting PM; Kaeberlein M

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Mice got rapamycin for only 3 months, starting at 20 to 21 months of age, and were then taken off it. A high injected dose (8 mg/kg a day) raised the males' remaining life expectancy after treatment by 60% (p = 0.02), which is a 16% longer median lifespan counted from birth. In females the same dose did not extend life (p = 0.26), and all 16 treated females examined had aggressive blood-cell tumours of the lymphoma type, against 6 of 12 controls, while other tumour types became rarer. A lower dose in the diet (126 ppm; the injected dose was estimated to equal about 378 ppm) raised post-treatment life expectancy by 42% in both sexes together and median lifespan by 13%, improved grip strength and rotarod performance, and changed the gut bacteria (more segmented filamentous bacteria). Boundary: mice only. The tumour counts come from small groups (12 to 16 per arm), side effects such as cataracts or testis changes were not tested at the dietary dose, and 'life expectancy' is counted from the end of treatment, so it makes the gain look larger than the change in total lifespan.

studies.title: A randomized controlled trial to establish effects of short-term rapamycin treatment in 24 middle-aged companion dogs
studies.authors: Urfer SR; Kaeberlein TL; Mailheau S; Bergman PJ; Creevy KE; Promislow DEL; Kaeberlein M

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: A short 10-week course of low-dose rapamycin in healthy pet dogs caused no clinical side effects, and echocardiography suggested improved measures of heart function.

studies.title: Rapamycin administration in humans blocks the contraction-induced increase in skeletal muscle protein synthesis
studies.authors: Drummond MJ; Fry CS; Glynn EL; Dreyer HC; Dhanani S; Timmerman KL; Volpi E; Rasmussen BB

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Rapamycin given before resistance exercise blocked the early (1–2 h) post-exercise rise in human muscle protein synthesis, which was about 40% in the control group. Rapamycin also blocked the rise in ERK1/2 phosphorylation and blunted MNK1, so the authors conclude that mTORC1 drives the response only in part. The study measured acute protein synthesis, not muscle growth.

studies.title: Efficacy of sirolimus compared with azathioprine for reduction of acute renal allograft rejection: a randomised multicentre study
studies.authors: Kahan BD (Rapamune US Study Group)

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: The trial that established rapamycin (sirolimus) as an immunosuppressant in kidney transplant patients - its original, still-standard clinical use.

studies.title: Targeting mTOR restores tau-induced metabolic, mitochondrial, and cognitive deficits in a tauopathy mouse model
studies.authors: Tang Z; Guo M; Ding Y; Wen Y; Li B; Xiao Y; Ni R; Guan Z; Qi XL

evidence.label: Preprint, not peer-reviewed
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: In mice engineered to overexpress a phosphomimetic tau variant, one week of rapamycin partially mitigated tau-driven mitochondrial dysfunction and cognitive impairment in the Morris water maze - extends the mTOR-autophagy-neurodegeneration link (already seen with Huntington's) to a direct tau-phosphorylation mechanism relevant to Alzheimer's.

studies.title: Targeting ageing with rapamycin and its derivatives in humans: a systematic review
studies.authors: Lee DJW; Hodzic Kuerec A; Maier AB

evidence.label: Synthesis of human data
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Described by its authors as the first systematic review of rapamycin/rapalogs in humans for aging. Screened 18,400 articles, included 19 studies. Found improvements in immune, cardiovascular, and skin (integumentary) parameters; NO significant effect on endocrine, muscular, or neurological systems. No serious adverse events in healthy people, but more infections and raised cholesterol/triglycerides in people with age-related disease. This is the highest-tier human-evidence summary in the whole Atlas - it aggregates many individual human studies rather than reporting one.

studies.title: What is the clinical evidence to support off-label rapamycin therapy in healthy adults?
studies.authors: Hands JM; Lustgarten MS; Frame LA; Rosen B

evidence.label: Review — secondary literature, not a new result
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Narrative review + PhenoAge modeling of one cohort
studies.finding: A deliberately cautious review of low-dose rapamycin in healthy adults, and re-models one cohort using the PhenoAge biological-aging clock. Verdict: despite strong animal lifespan data, human evidence does NOT yet prove rapamycin delays aging in healthy people. A valuable counterweight to longevity-community hype - it holds the human evidence to a strict standard rather than over-reading promising signals.

studies.title: Structure of the FKBP12-rapamycin complex interacting with the binding domain of human FRAP
studies.authors: Choi J; Chen J; Schreiber SL; Clardy J

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: The crystal structure that showed HOW rapamycin works at the atomic level: one rapamycin molecule glues two proteins together - FKBP12 and mTOR's FRB domain - by plugging into two hydrophobic pockets at once. A textbook example of a small molecule acting as 'molecular glue' to force protein dimerization.

studies.title: Prolonged rapamycin treatment inhibits mTORC2 assembly and Akt/PKB
studies.authors: Sarbassov DD; Ali SM; Sengupta S; Sheen JH; Hsu PP; Bagley AF; Markhard AL; Sabatini DM

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: The molecular explanation for rapamycin's dark side. Short-term rapamycin only hits mTORC1, but prolonged treatment can also inhibit the assembly of NEW mTORC2 in susceptible cell types, reducing mTORC2 abundance and cutting Akt signaling over time. The wording matters: this is prevention of new assembly, not the dismantling of complexes already built, and the response depends on cell context and length of exposure. This is the mechanistic root of the insulin-resistance side effect later shown in mice (see Lamming 2012) - crucial for anyone dosing rapamycin for longevity.

studies.title: An ATP-competitive mammalian target of rapamycin inhibitor reveals rapamycin-resistant functions of mTORC1
studies.authors: Thoreen CC; Kang SA; Chang JW; Liu Q; Zhang Jianming; Gao Y; Reichling LJ; Sim T; Sabatini DM; Gray NS

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Dropped a bombshell: rapamycin does NOT fully block mTORC1. Using Torin1 (which jams the active site directly), the authors showed rapamycin leaves important mTORC1 jobs running - notably 4E-BP1 phosphorylation and autophagy suppression. This reframed a decade of rapamycin experiments and launched the search for complete inhibitors.

studies.title: Active-site inhibitors of mTOR target rapamycin-resistant outputs of mTORC1 and mTORC2
studies.authors: Feldman ME; Apsel B; Uotila A; Loewith R; Knight ZA; Ruggero D; Shokat KM

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: The parallel discovery to Thoreen 2009 (same year), from the Shokat lab. Their TORKinibs (PP242, PP30) block mTOR's active site, hitting both complexes and shutting down cap-dependent translation that rapamycin misses. Together these two papers established a whole new drug class beyond rapamycin.

studies.title: mTOR kinase structure, mechanism and regulation
studies.authors: Yang H; Rudge DG; Koos JD; Vaidialingam B; Yang HJ; Pavletich NP

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Solved the crystal structure of the mTOR kinase itself. Revealed why the active site is so hard to reach - it sits in a deep recess guarded by the FRB domain, which acts as a 'gatekeeper' letting substrates in. This structure explains at the atomic level exactly how FKBP12-rapamycin blocks access, and why activating cancer mutations cluster where they do.

studies.title: Rapamycin decelerates cellular senescence
studies.authors: Demidenko ZN; Zubova SG; Bukreeva EI; Pospelov VA; Pospelova TV; Blagosklonny MV

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Blagosklonny's key experiment behind his 'hyperfunction' theory of aging. When a cell's division is blocked but mTOR keeps driving growth, the cell tips into permanent senescence. Rapamycin uncouples the two - keeping arrested cells reversible instead of senescent. Direct evidence that mTOR actively drives the senescent state, not just passively accompanies it.

studies.title: mTOR regulates the pro-tumorigenic senescence-associated secretory phenotype by promoting IL1A translation
studies.authors: Laberge RM; Sun Y; Orjalo AV; Patil CK; Freund A; Zhou L; Curran SC; Davalos AR; Wilson-Edell KA; Liu S; Limbad C; Demaria M; Li P; Hubbard GB; Ikeno Y; Javors M; Desprez PY; Benz CC; Kapahi P; Nelson PS; Campisi J

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Explained HOW rapamycin calms 'inflammaging'. Senescent cells spew inflammatory signals (the SASP) that damage surrounding tissue and even feed tumors. mTOR powers this by translating IL1A, the cytokine at the top of the cascade. Rapamycin selectively shuts it down - and blocked senescent cells from fueling prostate tumor growth in mice.

studies.title: Rapamycin slows aging in mice
studies.authors: Wilkinson JE; Burmeister L; Brooks SV; Chan CC; Friedline S; Harrison DE; Hejtmancik JF; Nadon N; Strong R; Wood LK; Woodward MA; Miller RA

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Answered a crucial objection: does rapamycin really slow AGING, or just prevent the cancers that kill mice? By showing slower age-related change across many tissues (heart, liver, tendon, activity), it argued for genuine slowing of aging. Honestly reported harms too - more cataracts and testicular degeneration - making it a balanced landmark, not hype.

studies.title: mTOR is a key modulator of ageing and age-related disease
studies.authors: Johnson SC; Rabinovitch PS; Kaeberlein M

evidence.label: Review — secondary literature, not a new result
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: The landmark Nature review that put mTOR at the center of aging biology. Lays out the case that inhibiting mTOR extends lifespan across species and guards against a growing list of age-related diseases - while being candid that side effects currently block its use in healthy people. Excellent orientation map for the whole field.

studies.title: Efficacy and safety of sirolimus in lymphangioleiomyomatosis (MILES)
studies.authors: McCormack FX; Inoue Y; Moss J; Singer LG; Strange C; Nakata K; Barker AF; Chapman JT; Brantly ML; Stocks JM; Brown KK; Lynch JP; Goldberg HJ; Young LR; Kinder BW; Downey GP; Sullivan EJ; Colby TV; McKay RT; Cohen MM; Korbee L; Taveira-DaSilva AM; Lee HS; Krischer JP; Trapnell BC

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: MILES was a 12-month placebo-controlled trial of sirolimus in 89 women with lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), a rare lung disease driven by overactive mTOR. On placebo, lung function (FEV1) fell by about 12 ml a month. On sirolimus it held steady (+1 ml a month), a 153 ml difference over the year. In the next year nobody took the drug, and the sirolimus group's decline resumed in parallel with placebo, so the benefit lasted only while the drug was taken. Walking distance and gas-transfer capacity did not improve. Boundary: patients had fairly advanced disease (average FEV1 about 48% of predicted), many dropped out of the observation year, and mouth ulcers and rashes may have revealed who was on the drug. Sirolimus was held at a blood level of 5 to 15 ng/ml, so this was continuous dosing, not intermittent.

studies.title: Topical rapamycin reduces markers of senescence and aging in human skin: an exploratory, prospective, randomized trial
studies.authors: Chung CL; Lawrence I; Hoffman M; Elgindi D; Nadhan K; Potnis M; Jin A; Sershon C; Binnebose R; Lorenzini A; Sell C

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: A small human trial testing whether rapamycin can slow aging in a tissue you can actually see and biopsy - skin. Topical rapamycin significantly lowered the senescence marker p16 and raised collagen VII, with visible improvement in skin appearance. Early, small-scale evidence (17 of 36 completed) that topical rapamycin can reduce a senescence marker in human skin.

studies.title: A randomized control trial to establish the feasibility and safety of rapamycin treatment in an older human cohort: Immunological, physical performance, and cognitive effects.
studies.authors: Kraig E; Linehan LA; Liang H; Romo TQ; Liu Q; Wu Y; Benavides AD; Curiel TJ; Javors MA; Musi N; Chiodo L; Koek W; Gelfond JAL; Kellogg DL

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: A safety-first pilot RCT (n=25, ages 70-95) asking the basic question before any longevity trial: is daily rapamycin safe in healthy older people? Over 8+ weeks it was well tolerated with only minor red-blood-cell changes and - importantly - NO rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance in this short window. Groundwork for larger aging trials like PEARL.

studies.title: Inhibition of mTOR by rapamycin abolishes cognitive deficits and reduces amyloid-beta levels in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease
studies.authors: Spilman P; Podlutskaya N; Hart MJ; Debnath J; Gorostiza O; Bredesen D; Richardson A; Strong R; Galvan V

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Connected the longevity drug to a specific age-related disease. Long-term rapamycin prevented memory deficits and lowered toxic amyloid-beta in an Alzheimer's mouse model - and the benefit tracked with INCREASED autophagy in neurons. Suggested that the same autophagy boost that may slow aging could also help clear disease-causing proteins.

studies.title: Molecular interplay between mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), amyloid-beta, and Tau: effects on cognitive impairments.
studies.authors: Caccamo A; Majumder S; Richardson A; Strong R; Oddo S

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Revealed a vicious cycle: amyloid-beta RAISES mTOR activity, and high mTOR in turn blocks the autophagy needed to clear amyloid and tau - so the disease feeds itself. Rapamycin broke the loop in 3xTg-AD mice, rescuing memory and lowering BOTH amyloid and tau, with autophagy induction shown to be necessary for the reduction in amyloid levels.

studies.title: Chronic inhibition of mammalian target of rapamycin by rapamycin modulates cognitive and non-cognitive components of behavior throughout lifespan in mice.
studies.authors: Halloran J; Hussong SA; Burbank R; Podlutskaya N; Fischer KE; Sloane LB; Austad SN; Strong R; Richardson A; Hart MJ; Galvan V

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Asked whether the lifespan-extending dose of rapamycin harms or helps the aging BRAIN. Reassuringly, it enhanced learning and memory in young mice, prevented age-related cognitive decline in old ones, and even reduced anxiety and depression-like behavior - linked to boosted brain monoamines. Cognitive benefit, not cost.

studies.title: mTOR controls mitochondrial oxidative function through a YY1-PGC-1alpha transcriptional complex
studies.authors: Cunningham JT; Rodgers JT; Arlow DH; Vazquez F; Mootha VK; Puigserver P

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Showed mTOR isn't just about building proteins - it also runs the cell's POWER plants. mTORC1 drives mitochondrial gene expression and oxygen consumption through a YY1-PGC-1alpha transcriptional program; block mTOR with rapamycin and mitochondrial output falls. Explains part of why mTOR inhibition reshapes metabolism.

studies.title: Association of rapamycin treatment with the modulation of purine metabolism, reduced microglial inflammatory responses, improved mitochondrial energy metabolism, and alleviation of fatigue symptoms in ME/CFS subjects: pilot findings from phase-II observational study
studies.authors: Brooke Gile, Sarojini Bulbule, Mubaraq A Toriola, Brian T Ruan, Shabnam Marium, Anna Benko, Stephanie Grach, Michael Mueller, Lucinda Bateman, Jennifer Bell, Brayden Yellman, Jon Berner, Bela Chheda, David Kaufman, Gunnar Gottschalk, Avik Roy

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: In an uncontrolled phase-II pilot (no placebo), low-dose rapamycin was associated with reduced fatigue in ME/CFS. In plasma from responders, purine intermediates shifted, consistent with lower IMP dehydrogenase activity in PBMCs. Lab assays suggest that altered purines can impair mitochondrial metabolism and promote microglial inflammation; these links were not measured in patients.

studies.title: Biological limits of lifespan extension: evidence for a shift from pathway leverage to system-level buffering across species
studies.authors: Denisa Fv Pirscoveanu, Mihai-Cristian Papa, Britta Kaltwasser, Dirk M Hermann, Ulf Brockmeier, Andrea Cercel, Anthony Oliver, Johannes Gruillari, Marius Viorel Ionica, Aurel Popa-Wagner

evidence.label: Review — secondary literature, not a new result
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: mTOR/TOR pathway interventions achieve large lifespan extensions in simple organisms but face declining efficacy in mammals due to distributed multi-tissue buffering, redundancy, and pharmacokinetic complexity - proposing a unifying framework for the translational challenge of aging pathway targeting.

studies.title: LKB1/AMPK deficiency aggravates mitochondrial DNA leakage via mTOR-dependent mitophagy damage in liver injury sensitized by trichloroethylene.
studies.authors: Zhu L, Wan C, Li Z, Fan X, Liu Z

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: LKB1/AMPK deficiency exacerbates trichloroethylene-induced liver injury by impairing mTOR-regulated mitophagy and causing mitochondrial DNA leakage; rapamycin and AMPK activation are protective, nominating the LKB1/AMPK/mTOR axis as a candidate therapeutic target in mice; no human data.

studies.title: Rapamycin co-exposure fails to reduce cisplatin-induced damage in GC6-spg spermatogonial cell line.
studies.authors: Jibrin A, Mitchell RT, Lopes F

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Rapamycin did not protect a mouse spermatogonial cell line from cisplatin damage in vitro, unlike reports in female fertility models.

studies.title: Late-life rapamycin treatment reverses age-related heart dysfunction
studies.authors: Flynn JM; O'Leary MN; Zambataro CA; Academia EC; Presley MP; Garrett BJ; Zykovich A; Mooney SD; Strong R; Rosen CJ; Kapahi P; Nelson MD; Kennedy BK; Melov S

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Striking evidence that in mice mTOR inhibition doesn't just SLOW aging - it can partly reverse an established age-related phenotype. Giving rapamycin to already-old (24-month) female mice for 3 months improved aged heart function, reversing or attenuating age-related cardiac changes, with RNA-seq changes suggesting anti-hypertrophic and anti-inflammatory effects. Started late, still worked.

studies.title: Influence of rapamycin on safety and healthspan metrics after one year: PEARL trial results
studies.authors: Moel M; Harinath G; Lee V; Nyquist A; Morgan SL; Isman A; Zalzala S

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: The authors describe PEARL as the longest trial of rapamycin for healthy ageing so far: 48 weeks, once a week, ages 50 to 85, 114 people finished (40 on 5 mg, 35 on 10 mg, 39 on placebo). The question the trial was built to answer was visceral fat on a DXA scan, and that did not change. Most of what gets quoted comes from secondary results. Lean mass rose in women on 10 mg, and these women also reported less pain, but pain came from a questionnaire the authors did not list as an endpoint, and only eight women were in the 10 mg group, hence the very wide interval (odds ratio 28, 95% CI 2.4 to 324). Side effects were similar to placebo, with more stomach complaints on rapamycin. Bone density was the one signal pointing the wrong way: in the 5 mg group the odds of an improvement in bone mineral density were lower than on placebo (odds ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.93, p = 0.04), but 10 mg showed no change (odds ratio 1.00) and the comparisons between groups were not significant. Boundary: the capsules were compounded, and the authors found they reached about a third of the blood level of the commercial drug, so 10 mg here is closer to 3 mg of generic sirolimus. Dosing was self-reported, and the group was about two thirds men and health-conscious.

studies.title: Rapamycin-induced fatty liver in mice is attenuated by chloroquine co-treatment in an ERRα-dependent manner
studies.authors: B'chir W; Dufour CR; Andrzejewski S; St-Pierre J; Scholtes C; Giguère V

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Chloroquine co-treatment attenuates rapamycin-induced hepatic steatosis (a known mTORC1-inhibitor side effect) in mice, and this rescue depends on the nuclear receptor ERRα; RNA-seq shows chloroquine reverses rapamycin-driven upregulation of lipid-metabolism genes, with ERRα identified as a top transcriptional regulator of the effect.

studies.title: Diet-dependent, beneficial and adverse effects of rapamycin on life span of Drosophila melanogaster
studies.authors: Jackson LN; Boles AM; Frye CT; Patel IA; Mockett RJ

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Rapamycin's effect on Drosophila lifespan is highly diet-dependent: on a cornmeal/torula-yeast medium it was harmful in 19 of 26 experiments across 5 strains, but on a nutrient-rich brewer's-yeast medium it was beneficial in 8 and neutral in 14, with no significant harm. Effects on median lifespan ranged from -51.3% to +5.4%, varying by sex and strain; rapamycin was also toxic to development at 10-200 µM.

studies.title: Lifespan benefits for the combination of rapamycin plus acarbose and for captopril in genetically heterogeneous mice
studies.authors: Strong R; Miller RA; Cheng CJ; Nelson JF; Gelfond J; Allani SK; Diaz V; Dorigatti AO; Dorigatti J; Fernandez E; Galecki A; Ginsburg B; Hamilton KL; Javors MA; Kornfeld K; Kaeberlein M; Kumar S; Lombard DB; Lopez-Cruzan M; Miller BF; Rabinovitch P; Reifsnyder P; Rosenthal NA; Bogue MA; Salmon AB; Suh Y; Verdin E; Weissbach H; Newman J; Maccchiarini F; Harrison DE

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Genetically heterogeneous UM-HET3 mice, three test sites (ITP C2017 cohort)
studies.finding: NIA Interventions Testing Program C2017 cohort. In MALE mice, rapamycin plus acarbose started at 9 months produced a longer lifespan than either of the two prior ITP cohorts treated with rapamycin alone, suggesting the combination is more potent than its components used separately. In FEMALES the combination was neither better nor worse than rapamycin alone, which the authors relate to the limited survival benefit acarbose alone had shown in earlier female cohorts. Captopril gave a small but significant lifespan increase in females (4-5%). CAVEAT (important for how this is cited): the rapamycin-only comparison is HISTORICAL, against prior cohorts, not a concurrent rapamycin-only arm in the same experiment, so 'more potent than either component' is the authors' suggestion rather than a within-experiment randomised comparison.

studies.title: mTOR signaling regulates central and peripheral circadian clock function
studies.authors: Ramanathan C; Kathale ND; Liu D; Lee C; Freeman DA; Hogenesch JB; Cao R; Liu AC

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Proposes a geroprotective mechanism for rapamycin that the authors call direct genoprotection. In human T cells exposed to acute genotoxic stress, rapamycin and other mTOR inhibitors suppressed senescence not by slowing protein synthesis, halting cell division, or stimulating autophagy, but by reducing DNA lesion burden and improving cell survival. 'Genoprotection' as a general property of rapamycin is the authors' interpretation, and no clinical endpoint was measured.

studies.finding: Female C57BL/6J mice that started rapamycin at 20 months of age, 2 mg/kg once every 5 days, lived longer than control females.
