Boundary: this record rests on the abstract only. The size of the lifespan gain, any male data and any side-effect measurements in these old mice are not extracted yet. The separation claim comes from combining two mouse studies (ARR2015 used young males), not from a single experiment.

studies.title: Sex-stratified immune patterns across the canine lifespan and short-term responses to geroprotective interventions
studies.authors: Lai M; Xu F; Xu Y; Mironenkov A; Jin Y; Zhang S; Pan J; Li M; Deng B; Zhu JK; Lyu YX

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Dog (intact laboratory Beagles: 80-dog cross-sectional cohort ages 1-11; 24 young dogs for a 90-day intervention arm)
studies.finding: In 24 young Beagles given a 90-day course of rapamycin, the SGLT2 inhibitor canagliflozin, or dietary restriction, rapamycin produced the broadest shift in blood cytokines of the three, while a separate cross-sectional cohort of 80 Beagles aged 1-11 showed that immune aging in dogs is non-linear and sex-stratified rather than a steady decline. Dogs are an increasingly used translational model for geroscience because of their size and lifespan diversity, so this adds a rare canine data point to the rapamycin-immune-aging picture; the authors flag the intervention findings as exploratory given small group sizes and endpoint-only measurements.

studies.title: A mouse model of TSC1 reveals sex-dependent lethality from liver hemangiomas, and up-regulation of p70S6 kinase activity in Tsc1 null cells
studies.authors: Kwiatkowski DJ; Zhang H; Bandura JL; Heiberger KM; Glogauer M; el-Hashemite N; Onda H

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Tsc1 knockout mice (null embryos, heterozygotes); Tsc1-null mouse embryonic fibroblasts; rapamycin treatment of cells
studies.finding: The authors built a Tsc1 knockout mouse to model tuberous sclerosis. Embryos lacking both copies of Tsc1 died at mid-gestation because the liver failed to develop. Mice with one copy often developed kidney cystadenomas and liver hemangiomas; the hemangiomas were more common, more severe and more often fatal in females. Fibroblasts lacking Tsc1 showed persistent phosphorylation of S6K and its substrate S6 that rapamycin could reverse, and S6 phosphorylation was also high in kidney tumours from the mice. The authors suggested that blocking this pathway might help control TSC tumours. Boundary: mouse model and mouse cells; the rapamycin result is in cultured cells, and treatment of the mouse tumours was not tested here.

studies.title: Single amino-acid changes that confer constitutive activation of mTOR are discovered in human cancer
studies.authors: Sato T; Nakashima A; Guo L; Coffman K; Tamanoi F

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Cells expressing mTOR point mutants found in cancer genome databases; in vitro kinase assays
studies.finding: Screened point mutations from cancer genome databases and found two, S2215Y (large intestine adenocarcinoma) and R2505P (renal cell carcinoma), that kept mTOR signalling on even under nutrient starvation. mTORC1 purified from starved cells carrying the mutants still phosphorylated 4E-BP1 in vitro. Mutant cells had more S-phase cells (42.0% vs 28.2% for S2215Y) and resisted the shrinkage caused by amino-acid withdrawal. The mutants stayed sensitive to rapamycin. Boundary: overexpressed mutants in cultured cells; the mutations were found in tumour databases, their driver role in patients was not tested.

studies.title: Disruption of the p70(s6k)/p85(s6k) gene reveals a small mouse phenotype and a new functional S6 kinase
studies.authors: Shima H; Pende M; Chen Y; Fumagalli S; Thomas G; Kozma SC

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: p70/p85 S6K1 knockout mice; embryonic fibroblasts and liver from knockout mice; S6K2 cloning and kinase assays
studies.finding: Mice with the S6K1 gene disrupted were viable and fertile but smaller, with the growth effect strongest during embryonic development. Unexpectedly, ribosomal protein S6 was still phosphorylated normally after mitogen stimulation in knockout liver and fibroblasts, and in knockout fibroblasts S6 phosphorylation and the rise in 5'TOP mRNA translation were as sensitive to rapamycin as in wild-type cells. A database search identified a second S6 kinase, S6K2, which had mitogen-dependent and rapamycin-sensitive S6 kinase activity and was up-regulated in all tissues of the knockout mice examined, most of all in thymus. S6K2 can therefore partly compensate for loss of S6K1. Boundary: Mouse knockout and mouse cells. Body size and S6 signalling only; the 5'TOP result means S6K1 alone is not required in these cells, not that S6 kinases are irrelevant. Drafted from the abstract only.

studies.title: Ribosomal protein S6 phosphorylation is a determinant of cell size and glucose homeostasis
studies.authors: Ruvinsky I; Sharon N; Lerer T; Cohen H; Stolovich-Rain M; Nir T; Dor Y; Zisman P; Meyuhas O

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Knock-in mice with all five rpS6 phosphorylation sites mutated to alanine (rpS6P-/-); embryonic fibroblasts; pancreatic beta-cells; glucose tolerance tests
studies.finding: The authors made knock-in mice in which all five phosphorylatable serines of ribosomal protein S6 were replaced by alanine, so rpS6 could not be phosphorylated. Contrary to the then widely accepted model, translational control of 5'TOP mRNAs was unaffected. Fibroblasts from these mice made protein faster and divided faster, yet were smaller than wild-type cells, and rapamycin did not shrink them further, which points to rpS6 phosphorylation as a downstream effector of mTOR in cell-size control. Adult mutant mice also had smaller pancreatic beta-cells, less pancreatic insulin, low blood insulin and impaired glucose tolerance. Boundary: Mouse knock-in and mouse cells. Separates rpS6 phosphorylation from 5'TOP control in these systems; not tested in people. Drafted from the abstract only.

studies.title: Rapamycin suppresses 5'TOP mRNA translation through inhibition of p70s6k
studies.authors: Jefferies HB; Fumagalli S; Dennis PB; Reinhard C; Pearson RB; Thomas G

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Mammalian cell lines (mouse 3T3 cells per MeSH); chimeric reporter mRNAs with intact or disrupted 5'TOP; dominant-interfering and rapamycin-resistant (T389E) p70s6k mutants
studies.finding: In mammalian cells, rapamycin selectively blocked the mitogen-induced increase in translation of 5'TOP mRNAs, which encode ribosomal proteins and elongation factors, and in parallel blocked activation of p70 S6 kinase. Using reporter mRNAs, the authors showed that an intact 5'TOP tract was required for the rapamycin effect. A dominant-interfering p70s6k reduced translation of the reporter with the intact 5'TOP but not the disrupted one, and a rapamycin-resistant p70s6k (Thr389 changed to an acidic residue) removed the inhibitory effect of rapamycin on 5'TOP translation. The authors concluded that rapamycin suppresses 5'TOP translation through p70s6k. Boundary: Cell lines with overexpressed kinase mutants and reporter mRNAs. Later genetic work (S6K knockouts, rpS6 knock-in) found 5'TOP control persisting without S6K1 or rpS6 phosphorylation, so the S6K step proposed here is not the current consensus. Drafted from the abstract only.

studies.title: Distinct perturbation of the translatome by the antidiabetic drug metformin
studies.authors: Larsson O; Morita M; Topisirovic I; Alain T; Blouin MJ; Pollak M; Sonenberg N

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Human cancer cell line (per MeSH); genome-wide polysome microarray translatome analysis comparing metformin, rapamycin and PP242
studies.finding: The authors compared genome-wide changes in mRNA translation caused by metformin with those caused by the mTOR inhibitors rapamycin and PP242 in cancer cells. Metformin changed gene expression at the level of translation to an extent comparable to the classic mTOR inhibitors. Its antiproliferative effect could be explained by selective suppression of translation of mRNAs encoding cell-cycle regulators, acting through the mTORC1 / 4E-BP pathway. The paper provided evidence that metformin's effect on cell growth in vitro goes through selective translational control rather than a general drop in protein synthesis. Boundary: Cultured cancer cells at drug concentrations used in vitro; does not show that metformin at clinical doses acts this way in patients. Drafted from the abstract only.

studies.title: The mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway regulates mitochondrial oxygen consumption and oxidative capacity
studies.authors: Schieke SM; Phillips D; McCoy JP; Aponte AM; Shen RF; Balaban RS; Finkel T

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Human Jurkat T cells (per MeSH); rapamycin; RNAi against TSC2, S6K1, raptor and rictor; subcellular fractionation; 2D-DIGE phosphoproteomics
studies.finding: In human cultured cells, the amount of mTOR-raptor complex correlated with overall mitochondrial activity. Disrupting the complex with rapamycin lowered mitochondrial membrane potential, oxygen consumption and ATP-synthetic capacity. mTOR and mTOR-raptor complexes were found in purified mitochondrial fractions, and rapamycin markedly changed the mitochondrial phosphoproteome. RNA interference against TSC2, S6K1, raptor or rictor led the authors to conclude that mTOR regulates mitochondrial activity independently of its previously known targets, and they proposed that mTOR activity shifts the balance between mitochondrial and non-mitochondrial ATP production. Boundary: Cultured human cell line with acute pharmacological and RNAi manipulation; the link to lifespan is a hypothesis drawn from lower organisms, not tested here. Drafted from the abstract only.

studies.title: siRNA screening of the kinome identifies ULK1 as a multidomain modulator of autophagy
studies.authors: Chan EY; Kir S; Tooze SA

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: HEK293 cells (GFP-LC3 lipidation assay, kinome siRNA library); HeLa cells; rat ULK1 constructs
studies.finding: The authors screened a kinase-targeted siRNA library in human HEK293 cells, using lipidation of the autophagy marker GFP-LC3 after amino-acid starvation as the readout. ULK1 came out of the screen: knocking it down blocked starvation-induced autophagy, while knocking down the related kinase ULK2 did not. ULK1 knockdown also blocked autophagy induced by rapamycin, which fits ULK1 acting downstream of mTOR. Overexpressed ULK1 inhibited autophagy independently of its kinase activity, and the dominant-negative effect mapped to residues 1-351, while the conserved C-terminal domain was needed for ULK1 to reach cytoplasmic structures, some of them LC3-positive. One of the early papers to place ULK1 as a required kinase for starvation-induced autophagy in mammalian cells. Boundary: Cultured human cell lines with siRNA and overexpression; no whole-animal data. The link to mTOR rests on rapamycin-induced autophagy, not on a measurement of mTORC1 acting on ULK1. Drafted from the abstract only (no PMC full text).

studies.title: Regulation of TFEB and V-ATPases by mTORC1
studies.authors: Peña-Llopis S; Vega-Rubin-de-Celis S; Schwartz JC; Wolff NC; Tran TA; Zou L; Xie XJ; Corey DR; Brugarolas J

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Tsc2-/- vs Tsc2+/+ immortalized MEFs (serum-deprived, +/- rapamycin) with microarrays; Tsc1 floxed primary MEFs and mouse liver (Ad-Cre); myr-Akt prostate model with everolimus (public data); HeLa cells with TSC2/Raptor knockdown
studies.finding: Using Tsc2-null and wild-type mouse fibroblasts with and without rapamycin, the authors looked for genes whose expression follows mTORC1 activity and found 75 genes, enriched for subunits of the lysosomal proton pump (V-ATPase). mTORC1 also raised V-ATPase expression in mouse liver after Tsc1 deletion and in a prostate tumour model, through a transcriptional mechanism that needed the transcription factor TFEB: knocking down Tfeb cut the number of mTORC1-induced genes from 1146 to 424 probes, and about a quarter of mTORC1-induced genes depended on Tfeb. mTORC1 promoted albumin uptake (endocytosis) in a Tfeb- and V-ATPase-dependent way. In these serum-deprived cells, active mTORC1 (TSC loss) increased nuclear TFEB and rapamycin or Raptor knockdown reduced it, which is the opposite direction to the TFEB inhibition reported by later studies in fed or starved cells. Boundary: Mostly mouse and human cell lines under low serum; liver and prostate data are expression measurements. The direction of mTORC1 control over TFEB localisation here differs from later work and is condition-dependent.

studies.title: Structure of the human mTOR complex I and its implications for rapamycin inhibition
studies.authors: Yip CK; Murata K; Walz T; Sabatini DM; Kang SA

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Human mTORC1 purified from HEK-293T cells stably expressing FLAG-raptor; negative-stain and cryo-EM (26 A); antibody labelling; in vitro kinase assays on S6K1 and 4E-BP1 with FKBP12-rapamycin or Torin1
studies.finding: The authors purified intact, active human mTORC1 and solved its shape by cryo-electron microscopy at about 26 angstrom resolution. The complex is an obligate dimer with a rhomboid outline and a central cavity, held together by interlocking contacts between mTOR and Raptor; antibody labelling placed mLST8 at the outer 'feet' and PRAS40 next to Raptor. Exposing purified mTORC1 to FKBP12-rapamycin first added a bound density in about 10% of particles, then broke the complex apart, with virtually no intact particles left after one hour, while the ATP-competitive inhibitor Torin1 left it intact. In matching kinase assays, FKBP12-rapamycin blocked S6K1 phosphorylation quickly but 4E-BP1 phosphorylation only after at least 60 minutes, and Raptor-free mTOR still phosphorylated S6K1 (rapamycin-sensitively) but not 4E-BP1. The authors proposed that rapamycin inhibits the two substrates by different mechanisms. Boundary: Purified protein and low-resolution EM; the authors note that in cells rapamycin neither fully blocks 4E-BP1 phosphorylation nor dismantles mTORC1, so the disassembly model is an in vitro result.

studies.title: Rapamycin inhibits the secretory phenotype of senescent cells by a Nrf2-independent mechanism
studies.authors: Wang Rong; Yu Z; Sunchu B; Shoaf J; Dang I; Zhao S; Caples K; Bradley L; Beaver LM; Ho E; Löhr CV; Perez VI

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Mouse skin fibroblasts and WT vs Nrf2-knockout MEFs (H2O2- or bleomycin-induced senescence); human WI38 fibroblasts (replicative senescence, CRISPR Nrf2 knockout); WT and Nrf2-knockout mice given rapamycin 4 mg/kg i.p. every other day for 6 weeks
studies.finding: The authors asked whether the transcription factor Nrf2 is needed for rapamycin to hold back cellular senescence. In wild-type mouse fibroblasts exposed to hydrogen peroxide, rapamycin raised Nrf2, switched on autophagy and lowered the senescence markers p16 and p21, beta-galactosidase staining and the inflammatory secretory profile (SASP). In Nrf2-knockout cells rapamycin still lowered beta-galactosidase staining and the SASP, but no longer lowered p16 and p21 or activated autophagy; re-expressing Nrf2 restored those effects, and human WI38 cells with Nrf2 knocked out by CRISPR behaved the same way. In Nrf2-knockout mice given rapamycin (4 mg/kg every other day for 6 weeks, 8 mice per group), fat-tissue beta-galactosidase staining and pro-inflammatory cytokines fell while p16 did not, and rapamycin lowered STAT3 phosphorylation in lung tissue and WI38 cells. The study provided evidence that rapamycin's effect on the SASP can be separated from its Nrf2-dependent effect on cell-cycle arrest. Boundary: Mouse and human fibroblasts in culture plus a short 6-week dosing study in young Nrf2-knockout mice; mTOR inhibition was by rapamycin, which was given before and during the senescence trigger, so this is prevention of senescence onset rather than treatment of established senescent cells.

studies.title: Rapamycin increases lifespan and inhibits spontaneous tumorigenesis in inbred female mice
studies.authors: Anisimov VN; Zabezhinski MA; Popovich IG; Piskunova TS; Semenchenko AV; Tyndyk ML; Yurova MN; Rosenfeld SV; Blagosklonny MV

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Female 129/Sv inbred mice given rapamycin intermittently (2 weeks per month) from 2 months of age for life; survival, body weight, ageing-rate measures and spontaneous tumours
studies.finding: Female 129/Sv inbred mice received rapamycin intermittently, 2 weeks in every month, from 2 months of age for the rest of their lives. Treated mice gained less weight with age, showed a slower estimated rate of ageing, lived longer, with the gain most visible among the last survivors, and developed spontaneous tumours later. 22.9% of rapamycin-treated mice were still alive when the last control mouse died. The paper provided evidence that an intermittent rapamycin schedule can extend lifespan in a normal inbred mouse strain, adding to earlier results in genetically heterogeneous mice. Boundary: Female mice of a single inbred strain (129/Sv) only; drafted from the abstract only, so dose, group sizes and median-lifespan statistics are not given here.

studies.title: Health Effects of Long-Term Rapamycin Treatment: The Impact on Mouse Health of Enteric Rapamycin Treatment from Four Months of Age throughout Life
studies.authors: Fischer KE; Gelfond JA; Soto VY; Han C; Someya S; Richardson A; Austad SN

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Male and female C57BL/6J mice fed microencapsulated rapamycin (14 ppm) or empty capsules from 4 months of age until death (40 per sex per group); repeated longitudinal health assessments from 16 months
studies.finding: Mice of both sexes were fed rapamycin in their food (14 ppm, encapsulated) from 4 months of age until death, 40 per sex per group, and the same animals were tested repeatedly for health measures from 16 months of age. Some measures improved: females had stronger grip at all ages, females kept body mass and fat longer during late-life weight loss, and sleep fragmentation fell in males (with a trend in females). Others did not change, such as stride length and age-related cochlear damage, and male rotarod performance was worse. In body mass, percent fat and resting metabolic rate, rapamycin moved males and females in opposite directions. The study showed that lifelong rapamycin in mice affects healthspan measures in a mixed and strongly sex-specific way rather than improving health across the board. Boundary: C57BL/6J mice only, one dietary dose; survival was reported in a companion paper, not in this one, and mTOR activity was not measured here.

studies.title: Lifelong rapamycin administration ameliorates age-dependent cognitive deficits by reducing IL-1β and enhancing NMDA signaling
studies.authors: Majumder S; Caccamo A; Medina DX; Benavides AD; Javors MA; Kraig E; Strong R; Richardson A; Oddo S

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: C57BL6/129svj mice (n=20 per group): encapsulated rapamycin in food (14 mg/kg food) from 2 to 18 months, from 15 to 18 months, or control diet; Morris water maze; brain cytokines, p-S6K, NR2B and CREB phosphorylation
studies.finding: Mice were fed rapamycin in their food either from 2 months of age or only from 15 months, when age-related memory deficits were already present, and all were tested at 18 months in a water maze (20 mice per group). Mice treated from 2 months learned the hidden-platform location faster and spent more time in the target quadrant in the memory test (28.7 vs 21.3 seconds for controls), while mice started at 15 months did no better than controls. Both rapamycin groups had lower phosphorylation of S6K in the brain, a marker of mTOR activity. The improvement in the early-treated mice went together with lower IL-1beta in brain and hippocampus and higher phosphorylation of the NMDA receptor subunit NR2B and of CREB, which the authors propose as the route. Boundary: Mice of one mixed strain, normal ageing (not an Alzheimer model); the late-start arm showed no reversal of existing deficits, and the IL-1beta and NMDA links are correlations, not tested by blocking them.

studies.title: mTORC1 in the Paneth cell niche couples intestinal stem-cell function to calorie intake
studies.authors: Yilmaz ÖH; Katajisto P; Lamming DW; Gültekin Y; Bauer-Rowe KE; Sengupta S; Birsoy K; Dursun A; Yilmaz VO; Selig M; Nielsen GP; Mino-Kenudson M; Zukerberg LR; Bhan AK; Deshpande V; Sabatini DM

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: C57BL/6 mice on calorie restriction (60% of ad libitum intake, 4-28 weeks) or rapamycin; Lgr5-EGFP reporter mice; doxycycline-inducible Rheb transgene and inducible Tsc1 and Rictor deletion; intestinal crypt and sorted ISC/Paneth-cell organoid co-culture; Bst1 knockdown and cADPR
studies.finding: Mice kept on calorie restriction (60% of normal intake) had more intestinal stem cells and Paneth cells, the cells that form the stem-cell niche (Lgr5+ stem cells 5.6% vs 4.3% of crypt cells, Paneth cells 9.8% vs 6.7%), and their crypts were nearly twice as likely to form organoids. In co-culture, Paneth cells from restricted mice, not stem cells, carried the boost. Restriction lowered S6 and S6K1 phosphorylation in crypts, and feeding or insulin switched on mTORC1 in Paneth cells but not in stem cells; forcing mTORC1 back on during restriction (Rheb induction or Tsc1 deletion) cancelled the effect, while one week of rapamycin copied it and did not add to restriction. The niche signal ran through higher Bst1 in Paneth cells, an enzyme that makes the paracrine messenger cyclic ADP ribose, and knocking down Bst1 removed the restriction effect in culture. Boundary: Mouse intestine and ex vivo organoid assays; restriction started in young adult mice, and no lifespan or human tissue was studied.

studies.title: Enhancing CD8 T-cell memory by modulating fatty acid metabolism
studies.authors: Pearce EL; Walsh MC; Cejas PJ; Harms GM; Shen H; Wang LS; Jones RG; Choi Y

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Mice with T-cell-specific TRAF6 deletion (CD4-cre), OT-I TCR-transgenic adoptive transfer, Listeria monocytogenes-OVA infection, EL4-OVA tumour vaccine model, and activated mouse CD8 T cells in vitro after IL-2 withdrawal
studies.finding: Mice whose T cells lacked the adaptor protein TRAF6 mounted a normal effector CD8 T-cell response to Listeria infection, but the antigen-specific cells vanished during contraction and almost no memory cells formed. The TRAF6-deficient cells failed to activate AMPK and mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation when the growth factor IL-2 was withdrawn. Daily metformin restored fatty acid oxidation and memory formation, and also raised memory CD8 T-cell numbers in normal mice: in a tumour vaccine model 6 of 9 metformin-treated mice survived beyond day 33 against 1 of 8 controls. Daily rapamycin (1.5 mg/kg), used as a second drug that promotes fatty acid oxidation, likewise increased memory CD8 T-cell development and recall responses. Boundary: mouse only, one bacterial infection model and one transplantable tumour; the rapamycin arm is a secondary experiment and mTOR activity itself was not measured in these cells.

studies.title: The mTOR kinase determines effector versus memory CD8+ T cell fate by regulating the expression of transcription factors T-bet and Eomesodermin
studies.authors: Rao RR; Li Q; Odunsi K; Shrikant PA

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Naive mouse OT-I CD8 T cells (and STAT4-deficient OT-I) stimulated in vitro with antigen plus B7.1 and IL-12, with rapamycin, PI3K inhibition, insulin or 2-deoxyglucose; adoptive transfer into C57BL/6 recipients and E.G7 tumour challenge
studies.finding: Working with naive OT-I CD8 T cells stimulated by antigen plus B7.1, the authors showed that IL-12 both raised and prolonged mTOR phosphorylation and S6K1 Thr389 phosphorylation out to 48 hours, and that this required PI3K throughout and STAT4 for the late phase. Rapamycin, added at the start or only at 12 hours, blocked the sustained expression of T-bet and with it the heritable type I effector programme, while raising Eomesodermin and producing cells with a memory-precursor phenotype (CD62L high, KLRG1 low, Bcl-2 high). Restoring T-bet by a tamoxifen-inducible construct brought back IFN-gamma production and lowered Eomesodermin, which places T-bet downstream of mTOR in this system. After transfer, the rapamycin-treated cells persisted better, gave stronger antigen-recall responses, and more than 78 percent of recipients stayed tumour-free to day 120 against 50 percent fatality with IL-12-conditioned effector cells. Boundary: mouse CD8 T cells, one TCR-transgenic system with pharmacological mTOR inhibition in vitro before transfer; the transplantable E.G7 tumour is a model, not a treatment result in people, and the memory-precursor phenotype faded by day 40 after transfer.

studies.title: Cutting edge: distinct glycolytic and lipid oxidative metabolic programs are essential for effector and regulatory CD4+ T cell subsets
studies.authors: Michalek RD; Gerriets VA; Jacobs SR; Macintyre AN; MacIver NJ; Mason EF; Sullivan SA; Nichols AG; Rathmell JC

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Primary mouse CD4 T cells polarised in vitro to Th1, Th2, Th17 and inducible Treg, with rapamycin, metformin or the CPT1 inhibitor etomoxir; Glut1-transgenic and Glut1-myc knock-in mice; OVA-driven allergic asthma model with metformin
studies.finding: Comparing CD4 T cells grown under effector and regulatory conditions, the authors showed that Th1, Th2 and Th17 cells carry high surface Glut1 and are strongly glycolytic, while inducible Treg carry little Glut1, oxidise lipid at a higher rate and have more phosphorylated AMPK. Blocking lipid oxidation with etomoxir selectively suppressed Treg generation and left effector differentiation intact, whereas removing glucose blocked Th17 but not Treg. Both rapamycin and metformin raised fatty acid oxidation in stimulated CD4 T cells, and etomoxir prevented the Treg increase produced by rapamycin or TGF-beta, which ties the pro-Treg effect of mTOR inhibition to lipid oxidation. In a mouse asthma model, metformin lowered Glut1 on activated CD4 T cells and increased the proportion and number of Treg in draining lymph nodes, although airway responsiveness itself did not change significantly. Boundary: mouse cells and one mouse allergic-airway model; mTOR inhibition is pharmacological (rapamycin) and mTOR activity was not measured directly, so the mTOR arm is inferred from drug effects.

studies.title: The metabolic checkpoint kinase mTOR is essential for IL-15 signaling during the development and activation of NK cells
studies.authors: Marcais A; Cherfils-Vicini J; Viant C; Degouve S; Viel S; Fenis A; Rabilloud J; Mayol K; Tavares A; Bienvenu J; Gangloff YG; Gilson E; Vivier E; Walzer T

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: NKp46-cre x Mtor-flox mice (NK-cell-specific mTOR deletion) plus acute TAT-Cre deletion and adoptive transfer; poly(I:C) and MCMV or influenza infection; oral rapamycin (sirolimus, 100 ug/day) with an in vivo missing-self rejection assay; Seahorse metabolic profiling; human NK cells from healthy donors stimulated with IL-2 plus rapamycin, PP242 or Ku-0063794
studies.finding: This study separated two arms of IL-15 signalling in NK cells by dose: low IL-15 mainly phosphorylated STAT5 (EC50 about 1.5 ng/ml), while higher IL-15 was needed to switch on mTOR (EC50 about 5.3 ng/ml for S6 phosphorylation), and IL-15 was the only one of many tested stimuli that strongly raised pS6. Deleting mTOR in NK cells left bone-marrow numbers normal but blocked the CD11b-low to double-positive transition, cut proliferation about three-fold and left almost no mature NK cells in the periphery, with lower CD71, glucose uptake and about half the surface CD122 and CD132, so the receptor feedback is itself mTOR-dependent. In activation, mTOR-deficient NK cells failed to grow or raise nutrient uptake after poly(I:C) and made about half as much granzyme B, while IFN-gamma production in response to IL-12 plus IL-18 stayed normal. Oral rapamycin lowered pS6 and granzyme B in vivo and made rejection of MHC-class-I-negative target cells significantly less efficient, and mTOR inhibitors also blocked IL-2-driven granzyme B induction in human NK cells. Boundary: mouse genetics and mouse in vivo pharmacology, with the human arm limited to healthy-donor NK cells stimulated in culture; the clinical implication for patients on rapalogs is inference, not a measured patient outcome.

studies.title: Sterol regulatory element-binding proteins are essential for the metabolic programming of effector T cells and adaptive immunity
studies.authors: Kidani Y; Elsaesser H; Hock MB; Vergnes L; Williams KJ; Argus JP; Marbois BN; Komisopoulou E; Wilson EB; Osborne TF; Graeber TG; Reue K; Brooks DG; Bensinger SJ

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Mouse T cells with Cd4-cre-driven deletion of Scap (removing both SREBP1 and SREBP2 activity), siRNA and constitutively active SREBP constructs, rapamycin and LY294002 pretreatment, ChIP for SREBP1/2 at lipogenic promoters, GC-MS lipid measurement, Seahorse profiling, LCMV-Armstrong infection and homeostatic-proliferation transfers
studies.finding: Activating T cells switch on cholesterol and fatty acid synthesis genes within hours, and this paper showed the switch runs through PI3K and mTOR to SREBP: 100 nM rapamycin given 30 minutes before stimulation blocked the induction of the lipogenic programme, prevented processing of full-length SREBP and its accumulation in the nucleus, and reduced SREBP1 and SREBP2 occupancy at lipogenic promoters to background. Deleting Scap in T cells, which removes both SREBP1 and SREBP2 activity, left thymic and peripheral T-cell numbers normal but the cells could not blast: they entered G1 and stalled, failed to raise cholesterol and fatty acids after activation, and increased ECAR and OCR only modestly where controls rose about ten-fold and four-fold. Adding cholesterol conjugated to methyl-beta-cyclodextrin roughly doubled survival at 48 hours (21 to 45 percent) and restored growth, cell-cycle entry and ER expansion, which points to cholesterol as the limiting step. After LCMV-Armstrong infection the Scap-deficient mice had fewer virus-specific CD8 T cells with lower IFN-gamma and TNF, while homeostatic proliferation was unaffected. Boundary: mouse genetics and mouse cells; the mTOR step is shown with rapamycin pretreatment in cultured T cells, and the in vivo arm measures the consequence of losing SREBP activity rather than of inhibiting mTOR.

studies.title: L-Arginine Modulates T Cell Metabolism and Enhances Survival and Anti-tumor Activity
studies.authors: Geiger R; Rieckmann JC; Wolf T; Basso C; Feng Y; Fuhrer T; Kogadeeva M; Picotti P; Meissner F; Mann M; Zamboni N; Sallusto F; Lanzavecchia A

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Human primary naive CD4 and CD8 T cells with high-resolution metabolomics, proteomics and limited-proteolysis mass spectrometry, plus CRISPR knockout T-cell clones; mouse HA-TCR transgenic transfers with oral L-arginine, and B16-OVA melanoma with OT-I transfer
studies.finding: Tracking metabolites and proteins in activated human T cells, the authors found intracellular L-arginine falls sharply after activation even in 1 mM medium, because uptake and conversion to ornithine, proline and spermidine rise. Raising L-arginine shifted metabolism from glycolysis towards oxidative phosphorylation, increased oxygen consumption and spare respiratory capacity, and produced central-memory-like cells (CCR7 and CD62L high, less IFN-gamma) with greater survival capacity; blocking arginase gave the same survival gain at physiological 150 uM L-arginine. Limited-proteolysis mass spectrometry plus knockout clones identified three nuclear proteins, BAZ1B, PSIP1 and TSN, that sense L-arginine and contribute to the survival programme. In mice, oral L-arginine raised serum levels from about 160 uM to 700 uM and roughly doubled intracellular L-arginine in activated T cells, and L-arginine-treated OT-I cells slowed B16-OVA growth and extended survival. The authors report explicitly that the survival effect was independent of mTOR: L-arginine did not change S6K1 or 4E-BP phosphorylation, and rapamycin, while also improving survival, changed metabolism in an entirely different way. Boundary: mostly human T cells in culture plus mouse transfer and transplantable-tumour models; the dietary arm is a mouse supplementation experiment, not a human trial, and mTOR enters only as a negative control.

studies.title: A rapamycin-sensitive signaling pathway contributes to long-term synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus
studies.authors: Tang SJ; Reis G; Kang H; Gingras AC; Sonenberg N; Schuman EM

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Rat and mouse hippocampal slices (field recordings, immunostaining); cultured rat hippocampal neurons; Western blot of rat hippocampus
studies.finding: The authors showed that mTOR, 4E-BP1, 4E-BP2 and eIF4E are present in rat hippocampus and sit in dendrites, close to synapses, where their staining overlapped with the postsynaptic protein PSD-95. Blocking mTOR with rapamycin in hippocampal slices reduced late-phase long-term potentiation (LTP) after high-frequency stimulation, while early-phase LTP was unaffected. Rapamycin also blocked the synaptic potentiation induced by the growth factor BDNF. This was one of the early papers to tie a rapamycin-sensitive pathway to the protein-synthesis-dependent phase of synaptic plasticity and to suggest it controls local translation at synapses. Boundary: rodent brain slices and cultured neurons; mTOR targets were localised but their phosphorylation during LTP was not reported in the abstract; no behaviour or memory test.

studies.title: Hypothalamic mTOR signaling regulates food intake
studies.authors: Cota D; Proulx K; Smith KA; Kozma SC; Thomas G; Woods SC; Seeley RJ

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Rats (Long-Evans): fasting/refeeding, intracerebroventricular leucine, leptin and rapamycin; hypothalamic immunostaining and Western blot
studies.finding: In rats, hypothalamic mTOR signalling (phosphorylated S6K1 and S6) changed with energy status in specific hypothalamic regions and was found in NPY and POMC neurons of the arcuate nucleus. Injecting leucine into the brain ventricles raised hypothalamic mTOR signalling and lowered food intake and body weight. Leptin also raised hypothalamic mTOR activity, and blocking mTOR with rapamycin in the brain blunted leptin's effect on reducing food intake. The authors proposed that hypothalamic mTOR acts as a fuel sensor linked to how much an animal eats. Boundary: rats, direct brain (intracerebroventricular) dosing, short-term food intake; drawn from the abstract only, so doses and effect sizes are not given here.

studies.title: Rapamycin alleviates toxicity of different aggregate-prone proteins
studies.authors: Berger Z; Ravikumar B; Menzies FM; Oroz LG; Underwood BR; Pangalos MN; Schmitt I; Wullner U; Evert BO; O'Kane CJ; Rubinsztein DC

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Mammalian cell lines (incl. COS cells) expressing polyglutamine- and polyalanine-expanded proteins; Drosophila expressing wild-type or mutant human tau
studies.finding: Building on their earlier work with mutant huntingtin, the authors showed in cell models that rapamycin, used as an autophagy inducer, increased the clearance of several proteins with long polyglutamine tracts and of a polyalanine-expanded protein, and reduced their toxicity. In fruit flies expressing wild-type or mutant human tau, rapamycin reduced tau toxicity, and this went with less insoluble tau. The authors argued that inducing autophagy with rapamycin could be useful across several aggregate-prone protein diseases, not only Huntington's disease. Boundary: cultured cells and Drosophila overexpressing disease proteins; drawn from the abstract only; no mammalian in vivo or human data.

studies.title: Autistic-like behaviour and cerebellar dysfunction in Purkinje cell Tsc1 mutant mice
studies.authors: Tsai PT; Hull C; Chu Y; Greene-Colozzi E; Sadowski AR; Leech JM; Steinberg J; Crawley JN; Regehr WG; Sahin M

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: L7Cre;Tsc1 flox mice (Purkinje-cell-specific heterozygous and homozygous Tsc1 deletion); cerebellar slice electrophysiology; behaviour; rapamycin from P7
studies.finding: Deleting one or both copies of Tsc1 only in cerebellar Purkinje cells raised phospho-S6 (a readout of mTORC1) in those cells. Both heterozygous and homozygous mutants showed autism-like behaviour: no preference for a mouse over an object or for a new mouse, more self-grooming, more pup ultrasonic calls and poorer reversal learning in a water T-maze. Purkinje cells fired fewer action potentials, both spontaneously and when driven, in a gene-dose-dependent way, while their synaptic inputs looked largely normal; homozygous mutants also lost Purkinje cells from about 2 months of age and became ataxic. Rapamycin (6 mg/kg intraperitoneally, three times a week from postnatal day 7) prevented the Purkinje cell loss and enlargement and the social, learning and motor deficits. Boundary: mouse, cell-type-specific genetic deletion; rapamycin given from early postnatal life, so this is prevention, not reversal; relevance to human autism is by analogy with TSC patients.

studies.title: Excitatory/inhibitory synaptic imbalance leads to hippocampal hyperexcitability in mouse models of tuberous sclerosis
studies.authors: Bateup HS; Johnson CA; Denefrio CL; Saulnier JL; Kornacker K; Sabatini BL

evidence.label: Molecular — cells, biochemistry, structure
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Tsc1 floxed mice: lentiviral Cre in dissociated hippocampal cultures (multi-electrode arrays, microarrays); CaMKIIa-Cre forebrain cKO (kainate seizures); sparse or widespread AAV-Cre in CA1 with slice electrophysiology; rapamycin in vitro and in vivo
studies.finding: Deleting Tsc1 from cultured mouse hippocampal neurons raised phospho-S6 and made the network fire more than twice as much as controls by day 14, in an epilepsy-like bursting pattern; four days of rapamycin brought activity back to control levels. Many gene-expression and synaptic changes in the knockout cultures, such as high Arc and fewer surface AMPA receptors, turned out to be secondary responses to the high activity, not direct effects of mTOR. In hippocampal CA1, Tsc1 loss in single pyramidal neurons weakened the inhibitory synaptic input they received and raised their excitation/inhibition ratio, while their intrinsic excitability was lower, not higher. Forebrain Tsc1 knockout mice had more severe kainate-induced seizures (80% died, while all controls survived), and seven days of rapamycin in vivo restored inhibition and normalised the E/I ratio. Boundary: mouse neurons, cultures and brain slices; Tsc1 deleted in excitatory neurons only; seizure test used a chemical convulsant.

studies.title: Rapamycin causes regression of astrocytomas in tuberous sclerosis complex
studies.authors: Franz DN; Leonard J; Tudor C; Chuck G; Care M; Sethuraman G; Dinopoulos A; Thomas G; Crone KR

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Humans: case series of 5 patients with TSC (4 subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, 1 pilocytic astrocytoma) treated with oral rapamycin, followed by serial MRI
studies.finding: Five people with tuberous sclerosis complex whose brain astrocytomas were growing on serial scans (four subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, one pilocytic astrocytoma) were treated with oral rapamycin at standard immunosuppressive levels (blood 5-15 ng/ml) for 2.5 to 20 months. On MRI, every lesion shrank, and one showed necrosis. In one patient the tumour grew back when treatment was interrupted and shrank again when it was restarted. Treatment was well tolerated. This small uncontrolled series was one of the early reports that mTOR inhibition can shrink TSC brain tumours in patients, and it preceded the EXIST-1 everolimus trial. Boundary: 5 patients, open-label case series without a control group; TSC-associated astrocytomas only; regression depended on continued treatment.

studies.title: Rapamycin prevents epilepsy in a mouse model of tuberous sclerosis complex
studies.authors: Zeng LH; Xu L; Gutmann DH; Wong M

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Mice: Tsc1(GFAP) conditional knockout (Tsc1 deleted mainly in glia) and littermate controls; rapamycin or vehicle from P14 (early) or 6 weeks (late); video-EEG, survival, histology, Western blot for phospho-S6
studies.finding: Mice lacking Tsc1 mainly in glial cells (Tsc1 GFAP conditional knockout) develop glial overgrowth, progressive epilepsy and early death. Rapamycin started at postnatal day 14, before symptoms, prevented epilepsy and premature death; started at 6 weeks, after seizures had begun, it suppressed seizures and prolonged survival. In the brain, rapamycin reversed the abnormal mTOR pathway activation (measured as phospho-S6), the astrogliosis and the neuronal disorganisation, and increased brain size, compared with vehicle-treated knockouts. The study provided evidence in mice that mTOR inhibition can act on epilepsy itself in TSC, not only on tumours, and it is part of the rationale for the later EXIST-3 seizure trial in patients. Boundary: mouse model with Tsc1 deleted mainly in glia, not the human germline mutation; seizure and survival outcomes in mice only; abstract does not state dose or schedule.

studies.title: Testing efficacy of administration of the antiaging drug rapamycin in a nonhuman primate, the common marmoset.
studies.authors: Tardif S; Ross C; Bergman P; Fernandez E; Javors M; Salmon AB; Spross J; Strong R; Richardson A
studies.journal: The Journals of Gerontology: Series A

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), oral Eudragit-encapsulated rapamycin, short-term (3 weeks) and long-term (14 months) studies
studies.finding: First description of dosing, pharmacokinetics, biochemical action and tolerability of rapamycin in the common marmoset. Eudragit-encapsulated rapamycin given orally at roughly 1.0 mg/kg/day gave mean trough blood levels of 5.2 ng/mL (range 1.93-10.73), comparable to rodent studies and within the human therapeutic range. In long-term animals (6 of 8) the phospho-rpS6 to total rpS6 ratio fell after 2 weeks, and rapamycin was detectable in liver and adipose tissue with reduced mTOR signalling there. There was no evidence of clinical anemia, fibrotic lung changes or mouth ulcers, and the death rate in the 14-month study was as expected for the animals' ages. Boundary: small cohort (6 of 8 long-term animals showed the pS6 drop), a 3-week and a 14-month study, pharmacology and tolerability only; no lifespan or healthspan outcome was measured, and nothing here is tested in people.

studies.title: Metabolic consequences of long-term rapamycin exposure on common marmoset monkeys (Callithrix jacchus).
studies.authors: Ross C; Salmon AB; Strong R; Fernandez E; Javors M; Richardson A; Tardif S

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), long-term oral encapsulated rapamycin, metabolic phenotyping
studies.finding: Long-term oral encapsulated rapamycin in marmosets had only minor metabolic consequences. Body weight was unchanged overall and fat mass fell only slightly over the first few months. Daily activity counts, blood lipids and glucose metabolism, including oral glucose tolerance, did not change significantly, and adipose tissue showed no difference in metabolic-marker gene expression. In liver, G6Pase activity was suppressed while PCK and GPI activity increased. Boundary: marmoset, oral rapamycin, metabolic endpoints only; the abstract gives neither the dose nor group sizes, and no lifespan result is reported.

studies.title: Pharmaceutical inhibition of mTOR in the common marmoset: effect of rapamycin on regulators of proteostasis in a non-human primate.
studies.authors: Lelegren M; Liu Y; Ross C; Tardif S; Salmon AB

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), oral rapamycin, liver, skeletal muscle and adipose tissue from a pilot cohort
studies.finding: In liver and skeletal muscle from rapamycin-treated marmosets (the earlier pilot cohort), rapamycin was associated with higher expression of PSMB5, a core 20S proteasome subunit, in both tissues but not of PSMB8; proteasome activity itself did not change. Mitochondria-targeted chaperones rose in skeletal muscle but not liver, and autophagy rose in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue but not liver. The authors conclude that only some components of the proteostasis network were upregulated, and in a tissue-specific way. Boundary: tissue samples from a small pilot cohort; the changes are expression-level associations and are not shown to cause any health or lifespan effect.

studies.title: Long-term treatment with the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin has minor effect on clinical laboratory markers in middle-aged marmosets.
studies.authors: Sills AM; Artavia JM; DeRosa BD; Ross CN; Salmon AB

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Middle-aged common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus), daily oral rapamycin, hematology and clinical laboratory markers, sex as a factor
studies.finding: In middle-aged marmosets given daily rapamycin, 9 months of treatment produced only minor changes in cellular blood counts, so hematological side effects are not likely outcomes of long-term rapamycin in relatively healthy middle-aged animals. Trough blood concentrations of rapamycin were significantly lower in females than in males, yet both sexes changed little. At baseline, males and females differed little in morphology or in markers of blood cell counts, metabolism and inflammation. Boundary: healthy middle-aged marmosets, 9 months, hematology and clinical laboratory markers only; it says nothing about efficacy or lifespan, and the abstract does not give the dose or group sizes.

studies.title: DNA methylation age analysis of rapamycin in common marmosets.
studies.authors: Horvath S; Zoller JA; Haghani A; Lu AT; Raj K; Jasinska AJ; Mattison JA; Salmon AB

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus) whole blood, DNA methylation array, rapamycin cohort; vervet and rhesus macaque for clock comparison
studies.finding: The authors built two epigenetic clocks for common marmoset blood from DNA methylation data; the human-marmoset clock for relative age correlated moderately well with age in vervet monkeys and rhesus macaques. In a separate marmoset cohort they tested whether rapamycin would change epigenetic age. The clocks did not detect a significant effect of rapamycin on the epigenetic age of marmoset blood. Boundary: a null result on one biomarker (DNA methylation age in blood). It does not show that rapamycin has no effect on aging in marmosets, only that these clocks did not register one; the abstract gives no dose, duration or group size.

studies.title: Rapamycin Attenuates Age-Related Changes in Marmoset Submandibular Gland: A Non-Human Primate Model of Human Oral Aging.
studies.authors: Abdul-Azees PA; Wang H; Chen J; Marinkovic M; Dean DD; Chen XD; Salmon AB; Yeh CK

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), chronic oral rapamycin, submandibular gland histology and immunofluorescence
studies.finding: In the aging marmoset submandibular gland the authors found fewer mucous and serous acinar units, expansion of ductal and collagen-rich stromal compartments, more extracellular matrix remodeling, dysregulated lipid metabolism, and more apoptotic and senescent cells. Chronic oral rapamycin was associated with partial preservation of acinar structure and with less fibrosis, lipid accumulation and fewer apoptotic and senescent cells, giving a tissue picture closer to that of younger animals. Boundary: histological and immunofluorescence associations in one tissue of a short-lived primate; the abstract gives no dose or group sizes, does not show that gland function improved, and reports no lifespan outcome.

relations.mechanism: Rapamycin is not an ordinary inhibitor: it first binds the small protein FKBP12, and only the two-part complex is the real drug.
relations.mechanism_beginner: Rapamycin doesn't work alone – it first has to team up with a helper protein called FKBP12.
relations.boundary: X-ray crystallography and in vitro work on bovine, rat and mouse material (CHO1996, BRO1994, SAB1995). Describes drug binding in purified systems; it says nothing about dose or effect in patients.
relations.note: The molecular-glue concept - genuinely surprising to newcomers.

relations.mechanism: The MILES trial: sirolimus stabilised lung function (FEV1) in lymphangioleiomyomatosis while patients took it, and decline resumed after stopping. This - not the everolimus angiomyolipoma trial - is the evidence that mTOR inhibition treats LAM lung disease.
relations.mechanism_beginner: In a clinical trial, rapamycin stabilised lung function in a rare lung disease while patients kept taking it – the decline came back once they stopped.
relations.boundary: Benefit is suppressive: lung function declined again after withdrawal.
relations.note: Added 2026-07-29. EVE-LAM previously carried this claim on a trial whose endpoint was renal angiomyolipoma.

relations.mechanism: Rapamycin extends lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice even when started late in life - one of the most influential results in the geroscience arm of this Atlas.
relations.mechanism_beginner: Rapamycin makes mice live longer, even when given late in life – the single biggest result behind the whole "this pathway and ageing" idea.
relations.boundary: Mouse only. No human lifespan or healthspan endpoint exists; EVERLAST has no results yet. BIT2016 shows a non-continuous schedule can still extend post-treatment life expectancy, but the result is dose- and route-specific: in the 8 mg/kg/day intraperitoneal arm males gained +60% post-treatment life expectancy (p=0.02) while females showed no survival benefit (p=0.261) and a shift toward aggressive haematopoietic cancers (16/16 vs 6/12, p=0.002); in the same paper's 126 ppm dietary encapsulated-rapamycin arm survival rose significantly in BOTH sexes, with a Cox model finding no evidence that sex modified the treatment effect (p=0.904). Cite the arm, not just the paper. ARR2016: an intermittent regimen (2 mg/kg every 5 days) started as late as 20 months of age extended lifespan in female C57BL/6J mice; the abstract reports the effect in females only.
relations.note: ARR2015 was removed from this edge on 2026-07-29: that study measured side effects only and has no survival endpoint.

relations.mechanism: Rapamycin does not touch mTORC2 in the short term - but over days it traps free mTOR and prevents new mTORC2 from being assembled.
relations.mechanism_beginner: Rapamycin doesn't touch mTORC2 right away, but over days it stops new mTORC2 from being built.
relations.boundary: Strictly time- and cell-type-dependent: absent acutely, present after prolonged exposure, and the sensitivity varies between cell lines. LAM2012 shows the same loss of mTORC2 signalling in mouse liver in vivo, so this is not a cell-culture-only phenomenon. Treating this edge as unconditional is a common error.
relations.note: THE key context-dependent edge. Should render dashed with an explicit 'chronic only' label. 2026-10-09: Interaction type changed complex-disassembly -> complex-assembly. Prolonged rapamycin prevents assembly of NEW mTORC2 (SAR2006); it does not disassemble existing complexes, so 'disassembly' was the wrong mechanism word. Sign stays 'inhibits' (it inhibits assembly).

relations.mechanism: Rapamycin inhibits mTORC1 only as a complex with FKBP12: the pair docks on the FRB domain beside the active site and blocks some substrates but not all, so S6K1 phosphorylation collapses while much of 4E-BP1 phosphorylation persists.
relations.mechanism_beginner: Rapamycin, carried by its helper protein FKBP12, jams part of mTORC1 – it blocks some of what mTORC1 does but not all of it.
relations.boundary: Directness is graded indirect because the mechanism requires FKBP12, as for everolimus and the bi-sterics. Acute effect only; the chronic effect on mTORC2 is the separate RAPA-MTORC2 edge.
